## Solution

We want to evaluate
$$I(a) = \int_0^1 \left(1 - x^{1/a}\right)^{-1/2} dx \quad \text{as } a \to 0^+.$$

**Substitution.** Let $x = t^a$, so $dx = a\, t^{a-1}\,dt$. The limits $x \in [0,1]$ map to $t \in [0,1]$, and $x^{1/a} = t$. Hence

$$I(a) = \int_0^1 (1-t)^{-1/2}\, a\, t^{a-1}\, dt = a\int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{-1/2}\,dt.$$

**Recognize the Beta integral.** The integral is
$$I(a) = a\, B\!\left(a,\tfrac12\right) = a\,\frac{\Gamma(a)\,\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac12\right)}{\Gamma\!\left(a+\tfrac12\right)}.$$

**Take the limit $a \to 0^+$.** Using the standard Laurent expansion of the Gamma function near zero,
$$\Gamma(a) = \frac{1}{a} - \gamma + O(a),$$
so $a\,\Gamma(a) \to 1$ as $a \to 0^+$. Also $\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac12\right) = \sqrt{\pi}$, and by continuity $\Gamma\!\left(a+\tfrac12\right) \to \Gamma\!\left(\tfrac12\right) = \sqrt{\pi}$ as $a \to 0^+$. Therefore

$$\lim_{a \to 0^+} I(a) = \lim_{a \to 0^+} \frac{a\,\Gamma(a)\,\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac12\right)}{\Gamma\!\left(a+\tfrac12\right)} = \frac{1 \cdot \sqrt{\pi}}{\sqrt{\pi}} = 1.$$

**Sanity check (boundary-layer intuition).** For $x \in (0,1)$ fixed, as $a \to 0^+$ we have $1/a \to +\infty$, so $x^{1/a} \to 0$ and the integrand tends to $1$. The only nontrivial contribution comes from a vanishing neighborhood of $x=1$; the substitution above shows this boundary layer contributes exactly the correction that pins the limit to $1$, consistent with the dominant-part value.

$$\boxed{\displaystyle \lim_{a \to 0^+} \int_0^1 \left(1 - x^{1/a}\right)^{-1/2} dx = 1}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
